idiom_name: typed transform function (template literals) / DOM XSLTProcessor
implementation_notes: TypeScript adds a typed signature to the JavaScript idiom: a pure function (artist: Artist) => string built from template literals and one escape helper, or a small builder returning a branded Html type; the DOM's XSLTProcessor (typed in lib.dom.d.ts) remains the declarative route in browsers, while Node has no XSLT. The classic transformer class is justified when one interface must serve several output formats.
pitfalls: The compiler cannot see markup: template literals are strings, so escaping and well-formedness stay runtime concerns - keep one escape helper and never interpolate raw user data.
XSLTProcessor is declared in lib.dom.d.ts only: excluding DOM libraries for a Node build removes the type, and the runtime does not exist there anyway.
Returning markup as string invites innerHTML insertion; a branded Html type plus a sanitizing insertion point makes the compiler enforce the escaping boundary.

variants.name: DOM XSLTProcessor
variants.implementation_notes: The declarative alternative where a DOM exists: XSLTProcessor.importStylesheet plus transformToFragment, typed through lib.dom.d.ts. Choose it when presentation is a stylesheet artifact and the data can be serialized to XML, accepting that the code only runs in a DOM environment.
pitfalls: The DOM types are ambient: in a Node build the XSLTProcessor type disappears and the transform must move to a build step or a native addon.
transformToFragment returns a DocumentFragment, not markup: serializing it back to a string with XMLSerializer loses the HTML parsing context.
